# Scholarship Batch 3 — Remaining Routes: Verified Portal & Fee + Gemini's Answers

**Scope:** All 109 routes on the scholarship board that were NOT covered in Batch 1 (18 routes, deadlines 2 Nov – 15 Dec 2026) or Batch 2 (22 routes, deadlines 16 Dec 2026 – 31 Jan 2027). Together, Batches 1–3 now cover every route card on the board.

**Part 1 — Verified portal, fee and deadline.** Checked 3 November 2026 against official sources only (university, government, funder and regulator pages). Where a fee or date could not be verified on an official source it is marked NOT FOUND — nothing is guessed.

**Part 2 — Gemini's answers (model output).** All 218 answers were collected on 3 November 2026 via the Gemini web app (Gemini 3.6 Flash, your signed-in account, one fresh chat per route, Q1 then Q2 in the same chat), at your instruction. "4 Argon" was locked behind a BDT 2,500/month Pro upgrade, so Flash was used throughout. Gemini's answers are ungrounded model output: useful explainers, but **where a Gemini answer conflicts with Part 1, Part 1 wins**. The most important conflicts are listed in the flags section below.

## 1. Paid US research post (J-1 or H-1B cap-exempt)

### Part 1 — Verified portal, fee and deadline (official sources, 3 Nov 2026)

- **Official application portal:** No single portal — this is a job route, not a degree. Posts are advertised and applied for employer by employer: USAJobs (usajobs.gov) for federal posts, university/hospital career pages for academic posts, and NIH institute pages for NIH posts. Once a host offers a post, J-1 sponsorship for physician researchers runs through ECFMG's Exchange Visitor Sponsorship Program (EVSP), applied for via MyIntealth (see the ecfmgj1 entry). There is no central application point for the route itself.
- **Application fee:** No application fee to search or apply for the posts themselves. Costs arise only at the visa/sponsorship stage if ECFMG sponsors the J-1 (ECFMG annual application fee $370 + SEVIS $220 + J-1 visa application fee — see ecfmgj1).
- **Key deadline / window (2027 intake):** None — rolling. Posts open and close year-round; the board's working advice is to start emailing PIs around May–July 2027 for a post-internship start.
- **Checked:** ECFMG EVSP pages (ecfmg.org / golive.ecfmg.org EVSP fees page) for the sponsorship leg; route structure as described on the board's own card (source: ecfmg.org, verified 1 Nov 2026).
- **Notes / flags:** UMBRELLA / JOB ROUTE — no single portal or deadline exists. Opens only after the internship (needs the conferred MBBS). J-1 Research Scholar via ECFMG is the safest visa leg; H-1B cap-exempt posts avoid the cap-subject fee issues but depend on the employer.

### Part 2 — Gemini's answers (Gemini 3.6 Flash, web app, 3 Nov 2026 — model output)

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

Paid US Research Posts in the USA (J-1 or H-1B Cap-Exempt)

These are full-time, salaried research jobs at US universities, medical schools, teaching hospitals, or research institutes — not unpaid observerships and not a degree program. You are hired as a Research Fellow, Research Associate, or Postdoctoral Research Fellow to work in a Principal Investigator's (PI) lab or clinical research team.

What It Involves / Funds

You work 40+ hours/week on a specific research project, typically for 1-2 years (renewable).

Core work: Designing studies, recruiting patients, collecting and analyzing data, writing manuscripts, presenting at conferences, and applying for grants.

What it funds: It funds YOU. The host institution pays you a salary (not a scholarship or tuition fee).

Typical Salary Range (2025-2026): $55,000 - $75,000 USD per year for a Research Fellow (higher in expensive cities like Boston, New York, San Francisco).

Benefits: Usually includes health insurance and sometimes relocation support. It does NOT pay for your USMLE exam fees or your flights.

This is different from an MPH/PhD program, where YOU pay tuition. Here, the employer pays you.

Who Can Apply?

This is the most important part for you:

Eligibility: You must have completed your MBBS degree. Most positions require the degree to be completed before the start date. Some labs will accept you during your internship if you can show your degree will be awarded before you start.

No USMLE Required to Apply: This is the key advantage. You do NOT need to have passed USMLE Step 1 or Step 2 CK to get a research post. Most PIs hire based on your CV, research interest, and interview.

No Prior Work Experience Required: Fresh MBBS graduates are the primary target for these roles. Your internship counts as clinical experience, and any student research, publications, or presentations (even small ones) will make you stand out.

Visa Sponsorship: The university/hospital sponsors your visa. This is the main reason these posts are so valuable for IMGs.

2 Visa Types Explained

1. J-1 Research Scholar (Most Common)

Sponsored by: The university itself (via its International Office) or via ECFMG.

Duration: Up to 5 years total.

Pros: Easier and faster for universities to sponsor. No annual lottery or cap.

Cons: Subject to the 2-Year Home Residency Requirement (212e) for many doctors from Bangladesh. This means after your J-1, you must return to Bangladesh for 2 years before you can get a Green Card or H-1B, unless you get a waiver (usually through a Conrad 30 waiver by working 3 years in an underserved area after residency, or a hardship waiver).

2. H-1B Cap-Exempt (The Gold Standard, But Rarer)

Sponsored by: The university/hospital as your employer.

Duration: Up to 6 years.

Pros: This is a dual-intent visa. It does NOT have the 2-year home residency rule, and it allows you to transition directly to residency and a Green Card. It is also "cap-exempt" — meaning it is NOT subject to the annual H-1B lottery that private companies face.

Cons: Much harder to get. Universities must pay higher legal fees and prove they cannot find a US worker. Only well-funded labs and large academic medical centers (like Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic, Harvard affiliates) routinely offer it. Many PIs will only offer J-1.

Key Facts & Deadlines You Must Know

There is NO central deadline. This is NOT like the Match. Posts are advertised year-round, on a rolling basis, whenever a PI gets grant funding.

Where to find them: The main job boards are not the only place. You need to use:
1. Direct Lab Websites: Find PIs in your field (Public Health, Epidemiology, Global Health) at top universities and email them directly with your CV. This is how 70%+ of these jobs are filled.
2. Job Boards: Mayo Clinic Careers, Cleveland Clinic Careers, Mass General Brigham Careers, NIH Jobs, Indeed, LinkedIn.

Timeline for You:

Now (During Internship): Start emailing PIs. You can apply 6-12 months before you want to start.

After MBBS + Internship Completion: Most positions require you to have your final degree certificate and transcripts ready before the visa process starts.

Visa Processing Time: Once you get an offer, the J-1 visa process takes 2-4 months (DS-2019 form, embassy interview in Dhaka). H-1B takes 4-6 months.

Start Date Flexibility: Unlike residency, which starts only on July 1, research posts can start any month.

Budget Note: Your $30,000 budget is MORE than enough. You will not need to pay tuition. Your main costs will be: Visa fees (~$500-1,000), flights (~$1,200), and initial living costs for the first 1-2 months until your first salary arrives (~$3,000-5,000).

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

How a Paid US Research Post Is Relevant to You (And Its Catches)

For your specific goal — practising medicine in the USA (2029 Match) or Europe — a paid research post is arguably the single most strategic move you can make right now. It solves your three biggest problems at once: Money, US Experience, and Visa.

1. Relevance to Your USA Goal (2029 Match)

This is a direct accelerator for your Match application:

Solves the "No US Clinical Experience" Problem: Residency programs in the US heavily favor applicants with US experience. A 1-2 year research post at a US academic center gives you strong US Letters of Recommendation (LORs) from well-known US professors, which are often more valuable than a 1-month observership.

Publications Boost Your CV: For competitive fields, and especially for your interests in Public Health, Epidemiology, and Global Health, having 3-5 US publications from a known institution can offset the fact that you are an IMG from Bangladesh with no prior work experience.

Earn While You Prepare for USMLE: Unlike studying in Bangladesh, you will be earning $55,000-$75,000/year while you study for Step 1 and Step 2 CK in the evenings. This completely removes your $30,000 budget pressure.

Networking for Residency: If you work in a department at a hospital (e.g., Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, Public Health), you are inside the system. PIs often personally recommend their research fellows to their own residency program directors. Many IMGs match at the same hospital where they did research.

Visa Bridge: You get to live legally in the US for 1-2 years, which allows you to do US clinical observerships, attend conferences, and build contacts before you apply for residency.

2. Relevance to Your Europe Goal

This is where the relevance is LIMITED:

Not a Direct Path to Europe: A US research post does NOT help you get licensed in Europe. If you later decide to go to Germany, the UK, or Ireland, you will still need to pass their specific licensing exams (e.g., PLAB/UKMLA for the UK, Approbation for Germany) and meet their language requirements.

Indirect Benefit: It DOES help if you want to do an MPH or PhD in Europe later. A US research post with publications makes you a very strong candidate for funded MPH/PhD programs in Public Health or Epidemiology in the UK, Netherlands, or Sweden.

3. The Catches & Limitations (You Must Understand These)

Catch 1: It Is NOT Clinical Practice

You will NOT be allowed to examine patients, prescribe medicine, or work as a doctor during a research post. Your title is "Research Fellow," not "Resident." Your work is data, papers, and lab work. You will not be practising medicine, and this time does NOT count toward your residency training.

Catch 2: The J-1 Two-Year Home Rule (The Biggest Trap)

If you come on a J-1 Research Scholar visa, and you are subject to the 212(e) rule (which applies to most Bangladeshi doctors because of the Skills List), you CANNOT directly switch to an H-1B visa or a Green Card after your research.

You would need to either:
a) Return to Bangladesh for 2 years, OR
b) Get a waiver later (most commonly by matching into residency on a J-1 Physician visa and then getting a Conrad 30 waiver after residency by working 3 years in a rural/underserved area in the US).

This is manageable if you plan for it, but you must know it before you accept a J-1 offer. An H-1B cap-exempt post avoids this problem entirely, which is why it is so sought after.

Catch 3: It Does NOT Guarantee a Residency Match

A research post improves your chances dramatically, but it is not a guarantee. You still must pass USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK with good scores, get ECFMG certified, and apply through ERAS. If you spend 2 years doing research but fail to pass USMLE, you will have to leave the US when your visa ends.

Catch 4: It Can Delay Your Timeline If You Are Not Careful

Your goal is the 2029 Match. If you start a research post in late 2027, you could do 1 year of research (2027-2028) and apply for the 2029 Match while still in the US. This is perfect timing.

However, if you start in 2028 and commit to a 2-year post, you might miss the 2029 Match application window (which opens in September 2028). You must negotiate your start and end dates with your PI to align with the Match cycle.

### Part 2 — Gemini's answers (Gemini 3.6 Flash, web app, 3 Nov 2026 — model output)

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

Mayo Clinic Research Fellow Posts — Complete Guide

Mayo Clinic is one of the top-ranked hospitals in the world (consistently #1 in the US). A "Research Fellow" post at Mayo is not a clinical residency — it is a full-time, paid research position in a lab or clinical research department at Mayo Clinic in Rochester (Minnesota), Jacksonville (Florida), or Scottsdale/Phoenix (Arizona).

What It Is

You are hired as a Research Fellow (sometimes called Postdoctoral Research Fellow or Research Associate) to work for a Principal Investigator (PI) at Mayo Clinic.

You do NOT treat patients. You conduct research: designing studies, analyzing data, writing papers, and presenting findings.

It is a job, not a degree. You are paid a salary and you do not pay tuition.

What It Involves / Funds

Duration: Usually 1 to 2 years, renewable up to 3 years depending on funding.

Workload: Full-time (40+ hours/week), in-person at Mayo.

Research Areas Relevant to You: Mayo has huge departments in:
- Epidemiology and Public Health (Department of Quantitative Health Sciences)
- Global Health
- Clinical Trials and Outcomes Research
- Aerospace Medicine — Mayo Clinic is one of the few US centers with a dedicated Aerospace Medicine program and research in pilot health, space medicine, and human performance. This is extremely rare and directly matches your interest.

What It Funds / Pays:

Salary: As of 2025-2026, Research Fellows at Mayo earn approximately $65,000 - $80,000 USD per year (depending on experience and location). This is higher than the national average for research fellows.

Benefits: Mayo provides comprehensive health insurance, paid vacation, and access to Mayo's internal training, library, and research resources.

What It Does NOT Fund: It does not pay for your USMLE fees, your visa fees, or your flights to the US. You must cover initial relocation costs yourself (though your $30,000 budget is more than enough for this).

Who Can Apply?

Eligibility Criteria:

Degree Required: You must have completed your MBBS degree before the start date. Mayo typically requires the final degree certificate and transcripts at the time of hiring.

No USMLE Required: You do NOT need to have passed USMLE Step 1 or Step 2 CK to apply for a research fellow post. This is a major advantage for fresh graduates.

Experience: No prior work experience or prior publications are strictly required, but they are highly competitive. Ideal candidates have:
- A clear research interest matching the PI's lab
- Any student research, thesis work, or publications (even 1-2 is helpful)
- Strong English communication skills

International Applicants: Mayo regularly hires international medical graduates (IMGs) from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, and other countries for research fellow positions. You do not need to be a US citizen or permanent resident.

Visa: Mayo sponsors visas for international research fellows. The standard visa is the J-1 Research Scholar visa. Mayo also sponsors H-1B cap-exempt visas for some positions, but this is less common and decided by the department's budget and legal team.

How to Apply (This Is Critical)

There is NO single application portal with a fixed deadline for all posts. Mayo Research Fellow posts are hired directly by individual PIs.

1. Search the Mayo Clinic Careers Website: Go to jobs.mayoclinic.org and search for "Research Fellow" + your field (e.g., "Epidemiology", "Public Health", "Aerospace Medicine").

2. Direct Email to PIs (Most Effective Method): Identify PIs at Mayo working in your area (use Mayo Clinic's faculty directory or PubMed to find their recent papers). Send a personalized email with:
- A short introduction (MBBS graduate from Bangladesh, interests in epidemiology/global health)
- Your CV (1-2 pages)
- A brief statement of why you want to work in their lab specifically

3. Interview: If interested, the PI will schedule a Zoom interview. This is usually 1-2 rounds.

Key Facts & Deadlines

No Central Deadline: Positions are posted year-round on a rolling basis, as soon as a PI receives grant funding. A post can be filled within 2-4 weeks of being posted, so you must check weekly.

Application Timing for You:

Start Now: You can start contacting PIs during your internship (late 2026 / early 2027), even before your final degree is in hand, as long as you are clear about your graduation date (September 2026 results).

Ideal Start Date: Most fellows start between July and September, but start dates are flexible year-round.

Visa Processing: After you receive an offer, Mayo's International Office will issue your DS-2019 (for J-1) or H-1B petition. This process takes 3-5 months, so you should factor this into your timeline. You will need to attend a visa interview at the US Embassy in Dhaka.

Competitiveness: Mayo is extremely competitive. Hundreds of IMGs apply for each post. A generic email will be ignored. Your email must show you have read the PI's work and can explain how your skills fit their lab.

Why Mayo Specifically Matters for You

Brand Value for Residency: Having "Mayo Clinic" on your CV is one of the strongest signals for US residency program directors. A Mayo LOR is often weighted more heavily than LORs from lesser-known hospitals.

Aerospace Medicine: If you are serious about aerospace medicine, Mayo is one of the only places in the US where you can do dedicated research in this field outside of NASA or the military. Mayo's Aerospace Medicine and Vestibular Research Lab is world-renowned.

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

How Mayo Clinic Research Fellow Posts Are Relevant to You (And the Catches)

For your specific profile — MBBS (2019-20 session, final results September 2026), currently interning in Chattogram, no prior work experience, $30,000 budget, aiming for the 2029 US Match or Europe, with interests in public health, epidemiology, global health, clinical research, and aerospace medicine — a Mayo Research Fellow post is one of the highest-value moves you can make. It is also one of the most competitive.

1. Relevance to Your USA Goal (2029 Match)

This is where Mayo gives you the biggest advantage:

A. It Solves Your Biggest Weakness: No US Experience

As a fresh IMG with no prior work experience, your biggest disadvantage in the Match is lack of US Letters of Recommendation (LORs) and US clinical/research exposure. A 1-2 year post at Mayo directly solves this:
- You get 2-3 strong LORs from Mayo faculty, who are well-known to residency program directors across the US.
- You get US publications (Mayo fellows typically publish 3-6 papers in 1-2 years), which is critical for competitive specialties and for public health / preventive medicine.

B. It Pays You While You Prepare for USMLE

Your $30,000 budget is not a constraint here. At Mayo, you will earn $65,000 - $80,000/year. You can study for USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK in the evenings/weekends while earning a full US salary. This is far better than staying in Bangladesh and spending your savings on exam fees and prep courses.

C. Perfect Timing for the 2029 Match

If you start at Mayo in mid-2027, you would have:
- 1 full year of Mayo research by September 2028 (when ERAS applications open for the 2029 Match)
- Time to complete Step 1 and Step 2 CK and get ECFMG certified before applying

This timeline aligns perfectly with your goal. Many Mayo research fellows match into residency at Mayo itself or at other top programs, partly because their PI advocates for them internally.

D. Direct Fit for Your Interests

Public Health / Epidemiology / Global Health: Mayo's Department of Quantitative Health Sciences and Center for Clinical and Translational Science are leaders in epidemiology and outcomes research. This is a direct match.

Aerospace Medicine: This is the unique advantage. Very few IMGs can access aerospace medicine research. Mayo's Aerospace Medicine program is one of the only civilian programs in the US. If you secure a post here, you would be in an extremely niche and valuable field.

2. Relevance to Your Europe Goal

Limited, but not zero:

Not a Licensing Shortcut: A Mayo research post does NOT help you get licensed in Europe. You would still need to pass PLAB/UKMLA (UK), Approbation (Germany), or other national exams, plus language requirements.

Strong for European MPH/PhD: If you later decide to do a funded MPH or PhD in Public Health/Epidemiology in Europe (e.g., UK, Netherlands, Sweden), a Mayo research fellowship with publications makes you an exceptionally strong candidate for scholarships. European universities highly value Mayo experience.

3. Catches & Limitations (Critical for You)

Catch 1: Extremely Competitive — You Have No Prior Experience

Mayo receives hundreds of applications from IMGs, many of whom already have publications, an MPH, or prior research experience. As a fresh graduate with no prior work experience, you are at a disadvantage. You must compensate by:
- Sending highly personalized emails to PIs (not generic mass emails)
- Highlighting any student research, thesis, or presentations from your MBBS, even if small
- Showing a clear, specific interest in that PI's exact research area

Catch 2: It Is NOT Clinical Work

You will not be a doctor at Mayo. You will not examine patients, write prescriptions, or do clinical rotations. This is purely research.

Important Limitation: Clinical Research ≠ US Clinical Experience (USCE)
Residency programs distinguish between research experience and hands-on clinical experience (clerkships, sub-internships, externships). A Mayo research post is excellent, but it does NOT replace USCE. To maximize your Match chances, you should try to arrange 1-2 months of clinical observership/externship during or after your Mayo post, ideally at Mayo or a nearby hospital, to get a clinical LOR as well.

Catch 3: The J-1 Visa Trap (2-Year Home Residency Rule)

Most Mayo international research fellows are sponsored on a J-1 Research Scholar visa. If you are subject to the 212(e) two-year home residency requirement (which applies to many Bangladeshi physicians), you cannot directly transition to an H-1B visa or Green Card after your fellowship without either:
a) Returning to Bangladesh for 2 years, OR
b) Obtaining a waiver (most commonly via a Conrad 30 waiver after residency, by working 3 years in an underserved area).

This does NOT prevent you from matching into residency — you would simply match on a J-1 Physician visa (sponsored by ECFMG) — but it does affect your long-term immigration path. If Mayo offers you an H-1B cap-exempt position, take it if possible, as it avoids this rule entirely.

Catch 4: Timing Risk for the 2029 Match

Mayo posts are filled on a rolling basis, and visa processing takes 3-5 months. If you delay your applications until late 2027 or 2028, you risk:
- Not starting in time to get meaningful publications before September 2028 (ERAS opening)
- Having your fellowship overlap awkwardly with interview season (October 2028 - January 2029), when you will need time off for interviews

You must negotiate your start date and ensure your PI supports you taking time off for USMLE exams and residency interviews.

Catch 5: Location and Cost of Living

Mayo's main campus is in Rochester, Minnesota — a small city with cold winters (-20°C). While the salary is high, the location is isolated compared to Boston or New York. Jacksonville (Florida) and Scottsdale (Arizona) are warmer alternatives, but have fewer positions in epidemiology/public health.

Bottom Line for You

A Mayo Clinic Research Fellow post is not just relevant — it is potentially transformative for your US goal, especially for aerospace medicine and public health. It pays well, fits your $30,000 budget (you won't need to spend it), and aligns perfectly with the 2029 Match if you start in 2027.

However, it is not a guaranteed path. You must apply early, apply strategically to PIs in your exact field, and understand that it is research — not clinical practice — and that the J-1 visa has long-term implications you need to plan for.

For Europe, treat Mayo as a CV booster for MPH/PhD applications, not as a licensing route.

### Part 2 — Gemini's answers (Gemini 3.6 Flash, web app, 3 Nov 2026 — model output)

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar Sponsorship — Complete Guide

What It Is

ECFMG (Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates) is the US organization that certifies international medical graduates (IMGs) to enter US residency training.

However, ECFMG also acts as a Designated Sponsor for the J-1 Exchange Visitor Program for physicians.

ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar Sponsorship means ECFMG sponsors your J-1 visa so you can come to the US to do full-time research (not clinical training) at a US academic medical center, university, or research institute.

This is different from the more common ECFMG J-1 Physician sponsorship, which is for clinical residency/fellowship training. The Research Scholar category is specifically for non-clinical research.

What It Involves / Funds

You are hired as a Research Fellow / Postdoctoral Fellow by a US host institution (e.g., a university hospital).

Your work: Full-time research (lab research, clinical trials data analysis, epidemiology, public health research, etc.). You are NOT allowed to provide direct patient care.

Duration: Initial sponsorship is typically for 1 year, renewable up to a total of 5 years in the Research Scholar category.

Funding / Salary: ECFMG does NOT pay you. The host institution must pay you a salary that meets US Department of State minimums. As of 2025-2026, this is typically $55,000 - $75,000 per year, plus health insurance (which is mandatory for J-1).

Costs Paid by You:
- ECFMG Sponsorship Application Fee: ~$1,800 - $2,200 USD (paid by you or sometimes by the host)
- SEVIS Fee: $220 USD
- US Embassy Visa Interview Fee (DS-160): $205 USD
- Health Insurance: If not provided by the host, you must purchase J-1 compliant insurance ($2,000 - $4,000/year)

Your $30,000 budget is more than enough to cover these upfront costs.

Who Can Apply?

To be eligible for ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar sponsorship, you must meet ALL of these:

1. Medical Degree: You must have completed your MBBS degree. You cannot apply while still a student. Your final degree certificate and transcripts must be available before ECFMG will process your sponsorship.

2. Host Institution Offer: You must ALREADY have a formal offer letter from a US academic institution for a full-time research position. ECFMG does not find you a job — it only sponsors the visa after you have an offer. The host must be an accredited academic institution or research institute.

3. English Proficiency: You must demonstrate English proficiency, usually via OET Medicine, IELTS, or TOEFL scores, or by having completed medical education in English (which applies to most Bangladeshi MBBS programs, but you should confirm with ECFMG).

4. No Prior J-1 Research Scholar Time Used Up: You are limited to 5 years total in this category. If you have previously been on a J-1 Research Scholar visa, that time counts against your 5-year limit.

5. Intent to Return Home: The J-1 is a non-immigrant, exchange visitor visa. You must demonstrate intent to return to Bangladesh after your research, although in practice many physicians later transition to residency.

6. No USMLE Required: You do NOT need to have passed USMLE Step 1 or Step 2 to get Research Scholar sponsorship. This is a key advantage.

Key Facts, Rules & Deadlines

1. The 2-Year Home Residency Requirement (212e) — CRITICAL

Most physicians from Bangladesh sponsored by ECFMG for J-1 Research Scholar ARE subject to the 212(e) rule. This means after your J-1 program ends, you must return to your home country for 2 years before you can apply for an H-1B visa, L visa, or US Green Card.

Exceptions / Waivers: You can apply for a waiver later, most commonly:
- Conrad 30 Waiver: After you complete a US residency, you work 3 years full-time in a federally designated Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA).
- Hardship or Persecution Waiver: If returning home would cause exceptional hardship to a US citizen spouse/child.

This rule does NOT prevent you from matching into residency on a J-1 Physician visa, but it does block a direct path to permanent residency without a waiver.

2. No Direct Patient Care Allowed

As a J-1 Research Scholar, you are legally prohibited from engaging in clinical activities involving direct patient contact. You cannot examine patients, take histories for clinical care, or prescribe. Your role is strictly research. Violating this can result in termination of your J-1 status.

3. The 12-Month and 24-Month Bars

If you complete a J-1 Research Scholar program, you may be subject to:
- 12-Month Bar: You cannot start a new J-1 Research Scholar or Professor program for 12 months after completing a previous J-1 program of more than 6 months.
- 24-Month Bar: You cannot repeat the Research Scholar category for 24 months after completing a full 5-year Research Scholar program.

These bars do NOT apply to switching to a J-1 Physician (residency) visa — that is a different category.

4. Deadlines — There Is NO Fixed Deadline

ECFMG processes J-1 Research Scholar applications year-round on a rolling basis.

Timeline:
- Step 1: Secure a research offer (this is the hardest part, takes 6-12 months of emailing PIs)
- Step 2: Host institution initiates sponsorship via ECFMG's EVSP (Exchange Visitor Sponsorship Program) online system
- Step 3: ECFMG reviews and issues Form DS-2019 (Certificate of Eligibility) — typically 4-6 weeks after receiving a complete application
- Step 4: You pay SEVIS fee, complete DS-160, and attend a visa interview at the US Embassy in Dhaka — allow 2-3 months for interview scheduling and visa issuance
- Total Time from Offer to Arrival in US: 3-5 months

5. Why ECFMG Sponsorship vs. University Sponsorship?

Some large universities (Harvard, Mayo, Stanford) sponsor J-1 Research Scholars directly through their own International Office, without needing ECFMG.

Smaller universities, hospitals, and research institutes that do not have their own J-1 designation use ECFMG as their sponsor. ECFMG acts as the legal sponsor, while the host institution is your actual employer.

For you, the process is almost identical — you will work with the host's HR department, and they will tell you whether they use ECFMG or their own sponsorship.

6. Health Insurance Requirement

J-1 regulations require you (and any J-2 dependents) to maintain compliant health insurance for the entire duration of your stay, including medical evacuation and repatriation coverage. Failure to maintain insurance results in automatic termination of your J-1 status.

Bottom Line for Your Timeline

If you want to use this route, you should start emailing PIs in late 2026 / early 2027, aim to secure an offer by mid-2027, and plan to arrive in the US by late 2027. This gives you 1 year of US research experience before the September 2028 ERAS application window for the 2029 Match.

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

How ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar Sponsorship Is Relevant to You (And Its Catches)

For you — MBBS graduate (2019-20 session, final results September 2026), currently interning in Chattogram, no prior work experience, $30,000 budget, aiming for the 2029 US Match or Europe, interested in public health, epidemiology, global health, clinical research, and aerospace medicine — ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar sponsorship is not a standalone opportunity. It is the visa mechanism that makes a paid US research post possible.

Think of it this way: The research post is the job. ECFMG J-1 sponsorship is the visa paperwork that lets you legally take that job.

1. Relevance to Your USA Goal (2029 Match)

This is highly relevant, and in many ways, essential:

A. It Is Your Legal Entry Ticket to the US

Without J-1 sponsorship (either via ECFMG or directly via the university), you cannot legally work as a research fellow in the US. ECFMG sponsorship is what allows smaller universities and hospitals — which don't have their own J-1 program — to hire you. This vastly expands the number of labs you can apply to beyond just the big names like Mayo or Harvard.

B. It Lets You Earn While Preparing for USMLE

Like a standard research post, you will earn $55,000-$75,000/year while in the US. This means you can study for Step 1 and Step 2 CK without draining your $30,000 budget. Your budget is more than sufficient to cover the ECFMG fee (~$2,000), SEVIS ($220), visa fee ($205), flights, and initial living costs.

C. It Builds Your Match Application

A year of US research under ECFMG J-1 sponsorship gives you:
- US Letters of Recommendation from US faculty
- US publications in public health, epidemiology, or global health — directly matching your interests
- Networking contacts who can advocate for you during the Match

If you arrive in late 2027, you will have a full year of US research before ERAS opens in September 2028 for the 2029 Match. This is ideal timing.

D. It Does NOT Require USMLE First

This is the key advantage for a fresh graduate. You can secure a research post and get J-1 sponsorship before you have passed any USMLE exams. You can then take Step 1 and Step 2 CK while in the US, which is often easier due to access to US study resources and a US testing environment.

2. Relevance to Your Europe Goal

Very Limited:

A US J-1 Research Scholar visa has no direct value for European licensing. It does not help you meet UK PLAB/UKMLA, German Approbation, or other European licensing requirements.

Indirect Value Only: If you do 1-2 years of research in the US on a J-1 visa and publish papers, you become a stronger candidate for funded MPH or PhD programs in Europe in public health or epidemiology. European universities value US research experience, but the visa itself is irrelevant to them.

If your primary goal shifts to Europe, you should not pursue ECFMG J-1 sponsorship — you should focus directly on European licensing exams and language requirements instead.

3. Catches & Limitations (You Must Plan For These)

Catch 1: You Must Find the Job First — ECFMG Does Not Find It For You

This is the most common misunderstanding. ECFMG is not a job placement agency. It will not match you with a lab. You must independently email PIs, secure an offer letter, and only then does ECFMG process your visa. The hardest part is not the visa — it's getting the offer.

As a fresh graduate with no prior work experience, you will need to send 100+ personalized emails to PIs to secure 1-2 offers. This is normal for IMGs.

Catch 2: The 2-Year Home Residency Requirement (212e) — The Biggest Long-Term Catch

Most Bangladeshi physicians on ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar visas are subject to the 212(e) rule. After your research ends, you must return to Bangladesh for 2 years before you can get an H-1B visa or Green Card, unless you get a waiver.

What this means for you:
- You CAN still match into US residency after research — you would switch to a J-1 Physician visa (also sponsored by ECFMG, but for clinical training).
- You CANNOT directly switch from J-1 Research Scholar to H-1B after research without a waiver or fulfilling the 2-year rule.
- The most common waiver path is Conrad 30: After residency, work 3 years in an underserved area in the US.

You must factor this into your long-term plan if your goal is to permanently practise in the US.

Catch 3: No Clinical Work Allowed — It Does Not Count as US Clinical Experience (USCE)

As a J-1 Research Scholar, you are legally prohibited from direct patient care. Residency programs distinguish between research experience and hands-on USCE (clerkships, externships). A research post alone, even at a top institution, does not give you USCE.

To maximize your Match chances, you should try to arrange a separate clinical observership or externship (1-2 months) during your research period, if your host institution allows it and your visa status permits it (observerships are typically allowed as they are non-clinical shadowing, but you must check with your J-1 Responsible Officer).

Catch 4: The 12-Month and 24-Month Bars Can Trap You

If you complete a J-1 Research Scholar program and then want to do another research program later, you may be barred for 12 months (after a program >6 months) or 24 months (after a full 5-year program). This does not block you from switching to residency (J-1 Physician category), but it does block you from doing back-to-back research fellowships at different institutions without a gap.

Catch 5: It Is Temporary and Tied to One Employer

Your J-1 status is tied to your specific host institution and research project. If your funding ends, your PI leaves, or you are terminated, your J-1 status ends and you must leave the US (usually within 30 days) unless you transfer to another approved host quickly. You cannot freely change jobs like a US citizen could.

Catch 6: Your $30,000 Budget — Sufficient, But Not for Dependents

Your budget is sufficient for a single applicant. If you plan to bring a spouse or dependents on J-2 visas, you will need to show additional proof of funds (typically $5,000-$10,000 extra per dependent per year) and pay for their J-1 compliant health insurance, which can quickly exceed your budget.

How to Decide Which Path to Choose

1. If you want research experience only: Pursue ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar sponsorship after securing a research offer. It is the fastest legal route to the US without USMLE.

2. If you want to combine research with USMLE preparation: This is the ideal use case. Secure a research post, get J-1 sponsorship, arrive in the US in 2027, study for Step 1 and Step 2 CK while working, and apply for the 2029 Match from within the US. You can also apply via a Pathway to get ECFMG certified while in the US.

3. If you want to transition to US clinical training: You need a separate visa sponsorship for residency (J-1 Physician via ECFMG, or H-1B if the residency program offers it). Your Research Scholar time does not automatically convert to residency — you must apply through ERAS and Match separately.

Bottom Line for You

ECFMG J-1 Research Scholar sponsorship is not a scholarship or a job — it is the visa bridge that lets you take a paid US research job without having passed USMLE first. For your 2029 Match goal, it is highly relevant and strategically valuable, especially for building US publications and LORs in public health and epidemiology.

However, it comes with the 2-year home rule, a ban on clinical work, and the risk of being tied to one employer. If your long-term goal is permanent US practice, you must plan for a waiver (Conrad 30) after residency, and you must not confuse research experience with clinical experience.

To match by 2029, you should complete Step 1 and Step 2 CK first, then look for a research post that will not clash with your Match timeline.

### Part 2 — Gemini's answers (Gemini 3.6 Flash, web app, 3 Nov 2026 — model output)

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

What is USMLE & ECFMG Certification?

USMLE (United States Medical Licensing Examination) is a standardized three-step examination process required for any physician to obtain a license to practice medicine in the United States.

ECFMG (Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates) Certification is the official credential verifying that an International Medical Graduate (IMG) meets the medical science and clinical skill standards necessary to enter an accredited U.S. residency or fellowship program.

What it involves: It requires demonstrating basic science knowledge, clinical knowledge, clinical skills assessment, and English proficiency through designated exams and credential verification.

What it funds: It funds nothing. ECFMG certification is an evaluation, credentialing, and gateway process, not a scholarship, fellowship, or research grant. All costs (registration, examination, credential processing, and travel) are paid out-of-pocket by the candidate.

What it Involves (Core Components)

To earn ECFMG Certification and complete the licensing pathway, you must fulfill four main components:

Credential Verification (Form 186 / Primary-Source Verification): ECFMG verifies your medical school enrollment, transcripts, and final diploma directly with your medical institution.

USMLE Step 1: A computer-based examination testing foundational basic medical sciences (Anatomy, Physiology, Pathology, Pharmacology, etc.). It is graded as Pass/Fail.

USMLE Step 2 CK (Clinical Knowledge): A computer-based exam testing clinical diagnosis, management, and patient care principles. It provides a numeric score (passing score is 218). For IMGs, this score is a crucial metric for residency selection.

Clinical & Communication Skills (ECFMG Pathways + OET): Because USMLE Step 2 CS (Clinical Skills) was permanently discontinued, IMGs fulfill this requirement via:

OET Medicine (Occupational English Test): Demonstrates medical English proficiency.

An ECFMG Pathway (Pathways 1–6): Most fresh graduates qualify through Pathway 3 or 4 (if their school holds recognized accreditation) or Pathway 6 (clinical skills evaluation via Mini-CEX by licensed physicians).

USMLE Step 3 (Post-ECFMG Certification): A 2-day exam testing independent patient management. Although taken after earning ECFMG certification, IMGs often complete Step 3 before applying for the Match to improve competitive standing and qualify for H-1B visa sponsorship.

Who Can Apply?

To apply for USMLE Step 1, Step 2 CK, and ECFMG Certification as an IMG, you must meet the following criteria:

Medical School Recognition: You must be officially enrolled in or a graduate of a medical school listed in the World Directory of Medical Schools (WDOMS) with an active ECFMG sponsor note.

Timing of Application: You can sit for Step 1 and Step 2 CK while still a medical student (after completing basic science coursework) or after graduation.

No Prior Work Experience Required: Post-graduation clinical work experience is not a strict requirement for taking the exams or applying to residency, though clinical experience (e.g., your post-MBBS internship or U.S. clinical electives/observerships) is highly valued during residency selection.

Key Facts & Rules

7-Year Rule: Once you pass your first exam (Step 1 or Step 2 CK), you must complete all required USMLE examinations (and fulfill ECFMG requirements) within a 7-year window.

Exam Locations: USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK can be taken in international Prometric test centers (including Dhaka, Bangladesh). Step 3 must be taken within the United States or its territories.

Retake Policy: You cannot retake a passed examination to score higher. Failed attempts are limited (up to 4 attempts total per Step).

Critical Timelines & Deadlines for a Target Match Year

For candidates targeting a U.S. Residency Match (e.g., the 2029 Match):

Target Match Cycle Timeline (e.g., 2029 Match)
- Year -2 to Year -1: Complete Step 1 & Step 2 CK
- Late Spring / Early Summer: Pass OET & Apply for ECFMG Pathway
- August (Year Prior): ECFMG Certificate Issued
- September 15: ERAS Applications Submitted to Programs
- Oct – Feb: Residency Interviews
- Late February: Rank Order List Submitted to NRMP
- Mid-March (Match Week): Match Results Announced
- July 1: Residency Training Starts

Pathway Expiration & Renewal: ECFMG Pathways open annually in the summer for the upcoming Match cycle. Applications for Pathways usually close around January 31 of the Match year.

Residency Start: Medical residency programs in the United States universally begin training on July 1 of each year.

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

Given your context as a fresh MBBS graduate from Chattogram (final results September 2026, post-MBBS internship), your target of the 2029 U.S. Match, a $30,000 USD budget, and non-clinical interests (public health, epidemiology, global health, research, aerospace medicine), the USMLE and ECFMG process is directly relevant, but carries distinct catches and structural limitations.

Relevance to Your Medical Goals

1. USA Pathway (Primary Target — 2029 Match)

Direct Gateway: USMLE + ECFMG Certification is non-negotiable. You cannot enter ACGME-accredited residency, sit for Step 3, or obtain a state license without it.

Relevance to Non-Clinical / Specialized Interests:

Public Health & Global Health: Having ECFMG certification and Step 3 completed makes you significantly more competitive for Preventive Medicine / Occupational Medicine residency programs or clinical research fellowships in the U.S.

Aerospace Medicine: In the U.S., Aerospace Medicine is a specialty entered after completing at least one clinical year (PGY-1 / Internship in Internal Medicine, Emergency Medicine, or Family Medicine) or a full residency. To complete PGY-1 in the U.S., you must be ECFMG-certified.

2. Europe Pathway

Irrelevant for Licensing in Europe: ECFMG certification is an American credential. European countries (e.g., UK, Ireland, Germany, Switzerland) do not accept USMLE or ECFMG certification as a direct substitute for their national licensing routes (e.g., PLAB/UKMLA in the UK, Approbation in Germany).

Indirect Academic Value: If you choose to pursue an MPH (Master of Public Health) or PhD in Europe (e.g., UK, Netherlands, Sweden), having passed Step 1 and Step 2 CK can demonstrate academic rigor when applying for research assistantships, though it holds no formal legal standing for clinical registration there.

Catches & Limitations Specific to Your Context

1. Budget Constraints ($30,000 USD total)

Exam Costs: Registration fees for Step 1 (~$1,200–$1,300), Step 2 CK (~$1,200–$1,300), OET Medicine (~$450–$500), and ECFMG Pathway fee (~$945) total roughly $4,000–$5,000 USD just for exam registrations.

The "Hidden" Match Costs: The U.S. residency application process itself (ERAS token, applying to 100+ programs, NRMP registration, USMLE Step 3) typically costs $4,000–$7,000 USD.

Hands-on U.S. Clinical Experience (USCE): To match into U.S. residency, programs strongly prefer 2–3 months of U.S. clinical electives or externships with Letters of Recommendation (LORs) from U.S. physicians. Clinical rotations for IMGs often cost $2,000–$4,000 USD per month plus living expenses.

Verdict on Budget: $30,000 USD is sufficient to cover the USMLE, ECFMG certification, OET, 2–3 months of USCE, and ERAS application fees, provided you pass all exams on the first attempt without spending excessively on commercial prep courses.

2. ECFMG Pathway Requirements for Bangladeshi Graduates

Clinical Skills Pathway: Since USMLE Step 2 CS was discontinued, you must qualify via an ECFMG Pathway (most fresh graduates from Bangladesh register under Pathway 3, 4, or 6 depending on their school's accreditation or complete Mini-CEX evaluations) alongside passing OET Medicine.

Pathway Expiration: Pathway-based ECFMG certifications carry temporary validity for the Match cycle they are issued for. Once you enter an accredited U.S. residency program, your certification becomes permanently valid.

3. Aerospace Medicine & Research Reality

Funding & Visa Limits: Aerospace Medicine residency spots in the U.S. are extremely limited, highly competitive, and frequently restricted to U.S. citizens or permanent residents due to military/federal (NASA/FAA) funding ties.

Alternative Route: The most viable bridge using your budget is to apply for a research fellowship or an MPH program in Global Health/Epidemiology in the U.S. or Europe, clear your USMLE steps during that period, and transition into a Preventive Medicine or Internal Medicine residency by 2029.

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

For your specific profile — a Bangladeshi MBBS graduate finishing internship in 2026 with no prior work experience and a $30,000 budget — this combination is one of the most realistic fully-funded routes to Europe. Here is the complete breakdown:

1. The Two Parts Explained

MSc in Global Health
The MSc in Global Health is a 1-year, full-time English-taught Master of Science program offered by Maastricht University in the Netherlands.

What it involves: The curriculum moves away from purely clinical medicine and focuses on transdisciplinary global health — how social, economic, political, and environmental factors shape health outcomes.

Structure: It is a 60 ECTS program with a strong problem-based learning (PBL) approach, a hallmark of Maastricht. You study core modules on global health governance, health systems, and research methods, and you complete a thesis / research project, often with an international field component.

Start date: September only, once per year.

NL High Potential Scholarship
This is the university's flagship scholarship for talented students from outside the EU/EEA, funded jointly by the Maastricht University Scholarship Fund and the Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (the Holland Scholarship component).

What it funds (for 2025-2026, the most recent published cycle):
- Full Tuition Fee Waiver: Covers the full cost of the non-EU tuition fee, which is €20,400 per year for this program.
- Monthly Living Allowance: €1,400 per month for 12 months (this is paid by the NL Scholarship component, €5,000, plus the UM High Potential top-up).
- Insurance: Health and liability insurance for the duration of your studies.
- Visa Costs: The costs for your visa application are covered.
- Pre-academic Training: Includes a pre-academic training course.

Note: This is a highly competitive scholarship — only about 24 scholarships are awarded per year across the entire university for all master's programs, not just Global Health.

2. Who Can Apply?

- Non-EU/EEA Nationality: You must hold a nationality from a country outside the EU/EEA, Switzerland, or Suriname, and meet the requirements for a Dutch residence permit. Bangladesh qualifies.
- New to Maastricht: You must have never been enrolled in a degree-seeking program at Maastricht University before, and you must not be a participant in a dual-degree program.
- Academic Excellence: You must have been admitted to the MSc Global Health program. In practice, this means you must be in the top 5% of your graduating class — you need to upload a document proving this ranking. Your MBBS degree is your qualifying degree.
- Age Limit: You must not be older than 35 years old on 1 September 2026 (for the 2026-2027 academic year).
- English Language: Since you are not a native English speaker, you must meet Maastricht's English requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall with at least 6.0 in each section, or TOEFL iBT 90 (min. 20 in each section).
- No Prior Work Experience Required: This is a key advantage for you — the scholarship is awarded on academic excellence and motivation, not on years of work experience.

3. Key Facts & Deadlines

- Program Admission: Apply through Studielink + MyUM portal by 1 May 2026 (for Sept 2026 start).
- Scholarship Application: You MUST apply for the scholarship by 1 February 2026, which is BEFORE the program admission deadline. This is the most common reason applicants miss out.
- Motivation Letter: You must write a separate, 1-page motivation letter specifically for the scholarship, explaining why you are a high-potential candidate.
- Selection Results: Scholarship results are announced in April 2026.
- Important warning: You cannot apply for the scholarship unless you have already applied for admission to the program, so you must submit your Studielink application in January 2026 to be safe.

Bottom line for your budget: If you win this, your €20,400 tuition + ~€16,800 living costs for the year are covered. Your $30,000 budget would remain almost untouched, which is a huge advantage for your later USMLE costs.

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

This route is highly relevant as a stepping stone, but it has one major timing catch that could make it difficult for you. Here is the honest breakdown:

1. Where It Fits Your Profile: Strong Fit for Europe / Public Health
- It is a perfect match for your stated interests in public health, epidemiology, and global health. Unlike a purely clinical degree, this MSc gives you a formal European qualification in a field where Bangladesh, WHO, and NGOs are actively hiring.
- It solves your budget problem: With the scholarship, you do not need to spend your $30,000. This preserves your entire budget for USMLE exam fees, US clinical rotations, and visa costs later.
- It gives you a legal pathway to Europe: After graduation, you can apply for the Dutch Orientation Year visa (zoekjaar), which gives you 1 year to live and work in the Netherlands to look for a job. This is a much easier entry point into Europe than applying for jobs directly from Bangladesh.

2. Where It Does NOT Directly Help You Practise Clinical Medicine
- This MSc does NOT give you a license to practise medicine in the Netherlands or the EU. It is an academic degree, not a medical registration. To work as a doctor in the Netherlands, you would still need to pass the Dutch BIG registration process, which requires C1-level Dutch language proficiency and assessment of your MBBS degree by the Dutch authorities. This is a separate, multi-year process.
- For the USA, this degree does NOT replace USMLE. You will still need to pass USMLE Step 1, Step 2 CK, and obtain ECFMG certification to be eligible for the 2029 Match. The MSc does not count as US clinical experience (USCE), which residency programs value highly.

3. The Biggest Catch: The Timeline Problem
This is the critical limitation for you:
- Your MBBS final results are in September 2026. The NL High Potential Scholarship deadline for a September 2026 start was 1 February 2026 — seven months BEFORE you will even have your degree certificate.
- You cannot apply for the 2026 intake with a degree you have not yet received. Maastricht requires a completed degree (or a formal statement of expected graduation) for admission, and the scholarship deadline is extremely early.
- Realistic timeline: You would need to target the September 2027 intake, applying for the scholarship by 1 February 2027. This means a one-year gap after your internship, which you would need to fill with research, USMLE preparation, or work.

4. Other Catches / Limitations
- Extremely competitive: With only ~24 scholarships university-wide, you are competing against top students from all over the world, not just for Global Health. A top 5% ranking is a hard requirement.
- One-year duration is short: The program is only 12 months. You will need to start your job search or USMLE preparation almost immediately after arrival, as there is no time to settle in.
- No guarantee of a job or residency: The scholarship funds your study, but it does not guarantee employment, a Dutch work visa after the orientation year, or a US residency spot.

Bottom line: If your goal is to work in public health / global health in Europe, this is an excellent, low-cost route — but you must plan for the 2027 intake. If your primary goal is to become a licensed clinical doctor in the USA by 2029, this route will delay your USMLE timeline by at least a year, so you need to weigh that delay against the benefit of a free European degree and a year of European experience.

## 7. NIH Visiting Program (Visiting Fellow)

### Part 1 — Verified portal, fee and deadline (official sources, 3 Nov 2026)

- **Official application portal:** No central application portal. Visiting Fellows are selected lab by lab: candidates contact NIH principal investigators directly, browse institute postdoc pages (e.g. NIAID's Postdoctoral Research Training page, which also runs a Postdoc Application System for that institute), and use the NIH Office of Intramural Training & Education (OITE, training.nih.gov) as the official entry point. Once a lab selects a fellow, the NIH Division of International Services (DIS) processes the Visiting Program case — the fellow does not apply to DIS directly.
- **Application fee:** NOT FOUND — no application fee is stated on NIH's official pages, and there is no central application to pay for; approaching PIs and OITE registration are free. (J-1 visa-stage government fees would apply later — see ecfmgj1 for the equivalent fee stack; NIH sponsors its own fellows' J-1s through DIS rather than ECFMG.)
- **Key deadline / window (2027 intake):** None — rolling; positions are filled whenever a lab has an opening.
- **Checked:** NIH official pages — NIMH Fellowships and Training Programs and NIAID Postdoctoral Research Training (nih.gov institute pages), and NIH Division of International Services guidance on the Visiting Program (ors.od.nih.gov), read 3 Nov 2026.
- **Notes / flags:** ELIGIBILITY FLAG (already on the board as "Eligibility to confirm"): a Visiting Fellow must hold a doctoral degree with less than five years of relevant postdoctoral experience — whether the conferral timing of his MBBS satisfies NIH's doctoral-degree requirement at the point of application is the open question. This is a paid stipend training post, not a degree or a scholarship.

### Part 2 — Gemini's answers (Gemini 3.6 Flash, web app, 3 Nov 2026 — model output)

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

For your profile — a Bangladeshi MBBS graduate finishing internship in 2026, with no prior work experience — the NIH Visiting Program is a high-prestige research opportunity, but it is NOT a degree program and it is NOT a direct route to practising medicine in the USA. Here is the complete breakdown:

1. What It Is

The NIH Visiting Program is a program run by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) in Bethesda, Maryland (near Washington, DC). It allows foreign scientists and physicians to come to the NIH Intramural Research Program to conduct biomedical research in one of its Institutes or Centers (e.g., NCI, NIAID, NHLBI).

Visiting Fellow is the specific appointment type for postdoctoral-level researchers. You are not a student, and you are not an NIH employee — you are a Visiting Fellow (a type of trainee) working under an NIH Principal Investigator (PI).

What it involves: You work full-time in a lab or clinical research group on a specific project. This can include bench research, clinical trials, epidemiology, or public health research, depending on the lab. You are expected to publish papers, present at conferences, and contribute to the lab's research output.

Duration: Visiting Fellow appointments are typically for 1 to 2 years initially, and can be renewed up to a maximum of 5 years total.

2. What It Funds / Pays

This is a paid research position, not a scholarship. You receive a stipend (salary), not tuition funding.

- Stipend: For 2025-2026, the NIH Visiting Fellow stipend starts at approximately $68,000 - $75,000 per year for a postdoctoral fellow with 0 years of experience, and increases with experience. This is paid monthly.
- Health Insurance: You are eligible for NIH health insurance coverage (through the NIH Fellows health plan).
- Travel: In some cases, the lab may cover initial travel to the US, but this is not guaranteed and depends on the PI's budget.
- What it does NOT cover: It does not cover tuition (there is no tuition, as it is not a degree), USMLE exam fees, or your family's costs if they join you. You must also pay US taxes on your stipend.

3. Who Can Apply?

- Degree Requirement: You must hold a doctoral degree (PhD, MD, MBBS, or equivalent) by the time you start. Your MBBS qualifies as a doctoral-level degree for this purpose, but you must have completed your degree and internship before starting.
- Research Experience: In practice, most successful applicants have prior research experience, publications, or a strong research background. With zero prior work experience, you will be at a significant disadvantage compared to other applicants, though it is not a formal exclusion.
- English Proficiency: You must be proficient in English, as all research is conducted in English.
- Visa Eligibility: You must be eligible for a J-1 Exchange Visitor visa (Research Scholar category). The NIH will sponsor this visa. You cannot use a B1/B2 tourist visa for this program.
- Finding a Lab: This is the most important step — you do NOT apply to a central NIH admissions office. You must directly contact NIH Principal Investigators (PIs) whose research matches your interests and secure an offer from a lab willing to host you.

4. Key Facts & Deadlines

- No Central Deadline: There is no single application deadline. Labs hire on a rolling basis throughout the year when they have funding and a vacancy.
- Application Process: 1) Search the NIH Intramural Research Program website for labs in your field (e.g., epidemiology, global health, infectious disease). 2) Email PIs directly with your CV, a cover letter, and your research interests. 3) If a PI is interested, they will interview you and then initiate the formal Visiting Fellow appointment process through the NIH Office of Intramural Training & Education (OITE).
- Start Date: Flexible, depending on when the lab hires you and when your J-1 visa is processed (typically 3-6 months after the offer).
- Competition: Extremely competitive. NIH labs receive hundreds of applications from around the world for a single position.

Bottom line: This is a paid research job at the world's largest biomedical research institution. It is excellent for your CV and for US residency applications, but it is not a study program and it does not lead directly to a medical license.

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

This program is highly relevant as a CV-building step for the USA, but it has major catches for your specific timeline and goal of practising medicine. Here is the honest breakdown:

1. Where It Fits: Excellent for US Residency (2029 Match)
- Direct US research experience: US residency programs value US research experience and US Letters of Recommendation (LoRs) more than almost any other factor for IMGs. A 1-2 year Visiting Fellowship at NIH — the most prestigious research institution in the US — would be a massive boost to your ERAS application. It directly solves your "zero prior experience" problem.
- Networking and publications: You would work with top US researchers, publish in high-impact journals, and get LoRs from NIH PIs, which carry enormous weight with residency program directors.
- It pays you: Unlike a master's degree, you do not need to spend your $30,000 budget. You would earn $68,000-$75,000 per year, which covers your living costs in the US and allows you to save for USMLE and residency application costs.
- USMLE preparation time: While working at NIH, you can prepare for USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK, and you would be physically in the US, making it easier to arrange US clinical rotations (observerships/electives) during or after your fellowship.

2. Where It Does NOT Help You Practise Medicine
- This is NOT clinical practice: As a Visiting Fellow, you are a researcher, not a practicing physician. You cannot treat patients, prescribe medication, or work as a doctor in a US hospital under this appointment. You are not licensed to practise medicine in the US.
- It does NOT replace USMLE/ECFMG: You will still need to pass USMLE Step 1, Step 2 CK, and obtain ECFMG certification to be eligible for the 2029 Match. The NIH fellowship does not grant you ECFMG certification or a medical license.
- For Europe, it has limited value: While NIH research is respected globally, a US research fellowship does not give you a European medical license or a direct pathway to work as a doctor in Europe. You would still need to meet each country's separate licensing and language requirements.

3. Biggest Catches / Limitations
- The "no experience" problem: This is the biggest catch for you. NIH PIs typically hire fellows who already have research experience and publications. With zero prior work experience and no publications (as of now), you will struggle to get a PI to choose you over applicants with PhDs and multiple papers. You may need to first build research experience in Bangladesh (e.g., through publications during your internship) before applying.
- J-1 visa and the 2-year home residency requirement: Most NIH Visiting Fellows come on a J-1 visa, which is subject to Section 212(e) — the 2-year home residency requirement. This means after your fellowship, you may be required to return to Bangladesh for 2 years before you can apply for certain US visas (like H-1B or permanent residency). This could seriously disrupt your 2029 Match timeline if you are on a J-1 and need a waiver to start residency.
- No guarantee of a residency spot: The fellowship improves your application, but it does not guarantee a Match. You will still be competing as an IMG in the Match.
- Timing: You cannot start until after you complete your MBBS and internship (late 2026 at the earliest). The J-1 visa process takes 3-6 months, so a realistic start would be mid-2027. A 1-2 year fellowship would then run into 2028-2029, which overlaps directly with your 2029 Match preparation — you would need to balance full-time research with USMLE study and ERAS applications.

Bottom line: If your primary goal is the US Match, the NIH Visiting Fellowship is one of the best possible CV boosters — but only if you can secure a lab offer despite your lack of experience, and only if you carefully manage the J-1 visa issue. If your goal is to practise medicine in Europe, this route is less direct than a European master's degree, as it does not give you a European qualification or a European work visa.

### Part 2 — Gemini's answers (Gemini 3.6 Flash, web app, 3 Nov 2026 — model output)

**Q1: What is it, what does it involve or fund, who can apply, key facts and deadlines?**

For your profile — a Bangladeshi MBBS graduate finishing internship in 2026, with no prior work experience and a $30,000 budget — Erasmus Mundus is one of the most generous fully-funded options in the world, and it is a perfect fit for your interests in public health, epidemiology, and global health. Here is the complete breakdown:

1. What It Is

An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master (EMJM) is a prestigious, fully funded, high-level integrated Master's program funded by the European Union.

These programs are designed and delivered by an international consortium of at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries.

Instead of studying at just one university, you spend your Master's degree studying in at least two different countries, moving between partner universities each semester or year.

2. What It Involves & How the Program Works

- Consortium Structure: A grouping of top European and global universities delivers a single joint curriculum.
- Duration & Credits: Programs run for 12, 18, or 24 months (60, 90, or 120 ECTS credits).
- Degrees Awarded: Upon graduation, you earn either a single Joint Degree (issued on behalf of all partner institutions) or Multiple Degrees (one from each university you studied at).
- The Erasmus Mundus Catalogue: The European Commission maintains an active online database listing over 150 Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programs across all fields, from public health to engineering to humanities. You can search this catalogue by field, country, or university to find programs that match your interests.

3. What Does the Scholarship Fund?

The Erasmus Mundus scholarship is one of the most generous fully funded postgraduate awards globally. It covers:

- Full Tuition & Academic Fees: 100% of university tuition fees, administrative charges, and mandatory health insurance.
- Monthly Living Allowance: A monthly stipend (typically €1,400 per month) paid directly to you for the duration of the program.
- Travel & Installation Support: Travel costs to/from Europe and between host countries are covered or reimbursed.
- Visa & Administrative Costs: Visa costs and setup allowances in destination countries are factored into the scholarship.

4. Who Can Apply? (Eligibility Criteria)

- Open to All Nationalities: Students from any country in the world (EU and non-EU) can apply.
- Non-EU applicants fall under "Partner Country" candidates and receive the full international scholarship.
- Academic Background: You must hold a recognized Bachelor's degree (or equivalent undergraduate degree) in a relevant field. Your MBBS degree qualifies as a first degree for most health-related programs.
- Final-year students are eligible as long as they graduate before the Master's program begins in September.
- Prior Scholarship Rule: You cannot receive an Erasmus Mundus scholarship if you have already been awarded an Erasmus Mundus scholarship for the same level of study.
- Language Requirements: Most programs are taught entirely in English and require proof of English proficiency (typically IELTS 6.5 or TOEFL 90, though this varies by program).
- No Age Limit: There are no upper age limits or requirements for previous professional work experience, which is a major advantage for you.

5. Key Facts & Deadlines

- Application Window: Programs open applications between October and November each year for entry in the following academic year.
- Deadlines: Deadlines vary by program but generally fall between December 15 and mid-February.
- Application Limit: You can apply to up to 3 different Erasmus Mundus programs in the same application cycle.
- Application Fees: Most programs have no application fee.
- Results Announcement: Final selection decisions (scholarship awardees and waitlist) are typically released between March and May.
- Required Documents: Degree certificate/transcripts, CV (Europass format), Motivation Letter/SOP, 2-3 Academic Reference Letters, English Proficiency Certificate, and Passport copy.

6. Key EMJM Programs Relevant to Health & Medical Backgrounds

- Europubhealth+ (European Master in Public Health)
- EMJMD PHDA (Public Health Data Science & Analytics)
- TROPMED (Master in International Health / Tropical Medicine)
- BIOETHICS (Erasmus Mundus Master of Bioethics)
- Global Health / Epidemiology Interdisciplinary Programs

Bottom line: With a full scholarship, your $30,000 budget would remain untouched, and you would gain a prestigious European degree, international experience in 2-3 countries, and a strong network for your future career in public health or medicine.

**Q2: How is it relevant to you, given your context, for practising medicine in Europe or the USA — including catches?**

Given your background — an MBBS graduate from Bangladesh (completing internship late 2026), zero prior work experience, and a $30,000 budget — Erasmus Mundus is a high-value, low-risk option for your long-term goals, but it is NOT a shortcut to a medical license in the USA or Europe.

If your goal is to move toward the USMLE Match or clinical practice in Europe — an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's (EMJM) is a strategic stepping stone, but not a direct license to practise.

Here is the exact breakdown of how this program aligns with your career path, along with the critical catches you must keep in mind.

How Erasmus Mundus Benefits Your Strategy

1. Zero Financial Risk & Maximum Capital Savings
Your total self-funded budget is USD 30,000. Preparing for the USMLE route (USMLE Step 1, Step 2 CK, ECFMG certification, clinical electives/observerships in US, ERAS application fees, and flight/visa expenses) easily costs USD 12,000 to 18,000.
- An EMJM fully covers tuition, insurance, and travel, plus gives you a stipend of ~€1,400/month.
- You will not touch your USD 30,000 savings during the 2-year Master's, preserving 100% of your financial capital exclusively for your USMLE exams, rotations, and US Residency application fees.

2. Strong CV Enhancement for US Residency (2029 Match)
Match statistics show that International Medical Graduates (IMGs) with zero prior work experience and no US Clinical Experience (USCE) face higher filter rates.
- A prestigious European Master's in Public Health, Epidemiology, or Global Health (e.g., Europubhealth+) signals strong academic capability.
- It generates peer-reviewed research publications and global academic networking — two factors highly prioritized by academic US residency programs (Internal Medicine, Preventive Medicine, or Pediatrics).

3. Strategic Buffer & Step Exam Preparation Timeline
After finishing your internship in late 2026, jumpstarting a 2027–2029 EMJM gives you a structured 2-year window to sit for USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK while living in Europe, keeping your academic gap clean.

4. Pivoting to Non-Clinical European Careers
If you decide to pause clinical medicine, an Erasmus Master's opens direct doors to high-paying non-clinical roles in Europe, such as roles in WHO, EU public health agencies, NGOs, pharmaceutical companies, and health policy organizations.

Key Catches and Limitations

1. It Does NOT Grant a Clinical License in Europe
An Erasmus Mundus degree is strictly an academic qualification (MSc/MPH), not a medical licensing credential.
- The Catch: To work as a hospital doctor in Europe (e.g., Germany, Ireland, UK, Spain, France), you must pass that country's specific medical licensing exam and meet its language requirements (e.g., German B2/C1 for Germany).
- Completing an MPH in France or Spain does not allow you to treat patients in a hospital during or after the program.

2. USMLE / ECFMG Eligibility Depends Only on Your MBBS
The US Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) evaluates your eligibility for US residency based exclusively on your primary medical degree (MBBS from Bangladesh).
- Your Erasmus degree adds zero formal credit toward your ECFMG eligibility.
- The Catch: You must ensure your medical college in Chattogram is listed in the World Directory of Medical Schools (WDOMS) with an active ECFMG note for your graduation year (2026).

3. High Mobility Can Split Your Focus
EMJMs require you to move countries/universities every 6 to 12 months.
- Settling into new cities, managing visa conversions between Schengen states, and keeping up with high academic coursework can eat into the dedicated study time required to score 250+ on USMLE Step 2 CK.

4. Lack of US Clinical Experience (USCE)
While an EMJM provides European research experience, most US residency programs heavily prioritize Hands-on US Clinical Experience (USCE) and letters of recommendation from US-based physicians. You will still need to arrange US observerships or clinical externships during your Master's break or immediately after graduating.

Verdict & Strategic Pathway
If you intend to target the 2029 US Residency Match:
1. Apply for EMJM (Oct 2026 – Jan 2027 cycle): Focus on programs like Europubhealth+ or Erasmus Mundus in Public Health in Disasters.
2. During the Master's (2027–2029): Live on the EU stipend. Prepare for and pass USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK.
3. Summer/Graduation (2028–2029): Use your untouched USD 30,000 budget to self-fund 2–3 months of US clinical electives/observerships, pay for ECFMG certification, and submit your ERAS application in September 2028 for the 2029 Match.
